{{Short description|Circle derived from a triangle}}
__notoc__
[[File:Fuhrmann circle.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Fuhrmann circle]]
[[File:Fuhrmann circle triangle.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Fuhrmann circle with Fuhrmann triangle (red),<br/> Nagel point <math>N</math> and orthocenter <math>H</math> <br/> <math>|AP_a|=BP_b|=|CP_c|=2r</math>]]
In [[geometry]], the '''Fuhrmann circle''' of a [[triangle]], named after the German [[Wilhelm Fuhrmann]] (1833–1904), is the [[circle]] that has as a [[diameter]] the [[line segment]] between the [[orthocenter]] <math>H</math> and the [[Nagel point]] <math> N</math>. This circle is identical with the circumcircle of the [[Fuhrmann triangle]].<ref> Roger A. Johnson: ''Advanced Euclidean Geometry''. Dover 2007, {{ISBN|978-0-486-46237-0}}, pp.&nbsp;228–229,&nbsp;300 (originally published 1929 with Houghton Mifflin Company (Boston) as ''Modern Geometry'').</ref> 

The radius of the Fuhrmann circle of a triangle with sides ''a'', ''b'', and ''c'' and [[circumradius]] ''R'' is

: <math> R\sqrt{\frac{a^3-a^2b-ab^2+b^3-a^2c+3abc-b^2c-ac^2+c^3}{abc}},</math>

which is also the distance between the [[circumcenter]] and [[incenter]].<ref>{{mathworld|urlname=FuhrmannCircle|title=Fuhrmann Circle}}</ref>

Aside from the orthocenter the Fuhrmann circle intersects each altitude of the triangle in one additional point. Those points all have the distance <math>2r</math> from their associated vertices of the triangle. Here <math>r</math> denotes the radius of the triangles [[incircle]].<ref>Ross Honsberger: ''Episodes in Nineteenth and Twentieth Century Euclidean Geometry''. MAA, 1995, pp. [https://books.google.com/books?id=7vcrmWEV73AC&pg=PA49 49-52]</ref>
